title: What is the difference between Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink for complex stream processing) and Amazon Kinesis Analytics (SQL-only queries on streams): and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Kinesis Data Analytics (managed Flink) and Amazon Kinesis Analytics (SQL-only), and when do you use each
keyPoints: Managed Flink runs full Apache Flink applications with the complete stateful, event-time feature set.
SQL-only Kinesis Analytics offers simple streaming SQL with limited windowing, state, and extensibility.
The SQL-only service is a legacy path; AWS steers new workloads toward managed Flink.
Managed Flink supports DataStream API, Table API, Flink SQL, CEP, and rich connectors.
Managed Flink itself supports Flink SQL, so you get SQL-style logic with the full engine underneath.
Outgrowing the SQL-only service means a rewrite, so starting on managed Flink avoids future rework.
Choose SQL-only only for very simple, low-stakes transforms where its constraints are acceptable.

s1_definition.oneliner: Managed Flink runs full Apache Flink applications with the complete stateful, event-time feature set for complex production processing, while the legacy SQL-only Kinesis Analytics offers quick streaming SQL with limited windowing and state.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Managed Flink** – Runs full Apache Flink applications in Java, Scala, Python, or Flink SQL with the complete feature set.
- **SQL-only Kinesis Analytics** – A legacy service for simple streaming SQL directly against Kinesis streams, with limited capabilities.
- **Feature gap** – SQL-only lacks robust state management, event-time handling, complex joins, CEP, and rich connectors.
- **Strategic direction** – AWS steers new workloads toward managed Flink and encourages migration from SQL-only.
- **Flink SQL on managed Flink** – Gives SQL-style logic without the ceiling, making the SQL-only service largely redundant.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two tools for analyzing transaction streams. The SQL-only service is like a basic calculator on the counter: an analyst can type a quick sum and get an answer instantly, but it cannot do anything elaborate. Managed Flink is like a full engineering workshop: it can build any machine the bank needs, with memory of each customer, precise timers, and complex pattern detection. For a quick tally the calculator is fine, but for the real fraud engine the bank needs the workshop.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is managed Flink?

The managed Flink offering is the full Apache Flink runtime as a managed service. You write real Flink applications and get the entire model.

```java
package com.bank.flink.aws;

import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.environment.StreamExecutionEnvironment;
import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.CheckpointingMode;

public class ManagedFlinkFullFeature {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();
        env.setParallelism(4);
        env.enableCheckpointing(60000, CheckpointingMode.EXACTLY_ONCE);

        // Full Flink feature set available:
        // - Event-time windows with watermarks
        // - Keyed state with RocksDB
        // - Timers and process functions
        // - CEP and MATCH_RECOGNIZE
        // - Flink SQL and Table API
        // - Rich connector ecosystem
        // - Exactly-once end-to-end

        env.fromElements("fraud-check-001")
            .map(check -> "Scored: " + check)
            .print();
        env.execute("NBI-Full-Feature-Managed");
    }
}
```

```text
Managed Flink capabilities:
  ✓ DataStream API (Java, Scala, Python)
  ✓ Table API and Flink SQL
  ✓ Event-time processing with watermarks
  ✓ Keyed state (HashMap, RocksDB)
  ✓ Event-time and processing-time timers
  ✓ CEP library and MATCH_RECOGNIZE
  ✓ Temporal joins, windowed joins
  ✓ Async I/O
  ✓ Rich connectors (Kinesis, MSK, S3, JDBC, DynamoDB)
  ✓ Exactly-once with compatible sinks
  ✓ Elastic scaling with KPU autoscaling
```

### What is the SQL-only service?

The SQL-only Kinesis Analytics is a simpler service where you write streaming SQL directly against Kinesis streams without any Flink code.

```sql
-- SQL-only Kinesis Analytics example:
-- Simple tumbling window aggregate on a Kinesis stream
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM output_stream (
    branch_id VARCHAR(32),
    total_amount DOUBLE,
    window_end TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE OR REPLACE PUMP output_pump AS
INSERT INTO output_stream
SELECT STREAM
    branch_id,
    SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
    STEP(transactions.ROWTIME BY INTERVAL '1' MINUTE) AS window_end
FROM transactions
GROUP BY branch_id, STEP(transactions.ROWTIME BY INTERVAL '1' MINUTE);
```

```text
SQL-only limitations:
  ✗ No keyed state or RocksDB
  ✗ No event-time watermarks (processing time only)
  ✗ No complex joins or temporal joins
  ✗ No CEP or MATCH_RECOGNIZE
  ✗ No custom logic or UDFs
  ✗ Limited windowing (tumbling only, basic)
  ✗ No exactly-once guarantees
  ✗ Legacy path (AWS discourages new use)
```

### How do they compare?

| Feature | Managed Flink | SQL-Only |
|---|---|---|
| Programming model | Java/Scala/Python/SQL | SQL only |
| Engine | Apache Flink | Proprietary |
| State management | Full (keyed, RocksDB) | Very limited |
| Event-time processing | Full (watermarks) | Processing time only |
| Complex joins | Temporal, windowed, interval | Basic |
| Pattern detection | CEP, MATCH_RECOGNIZE | None |
| Connectors | Rich ecosystem | Kinesis only |
| Exactly-once | Yes (with compatible sinks) | No |
| Scaling | KPU autoscaling | Limited |
| Portability | Code runs on open-source Flink | Locked in |
| AWS recommendation | Strategic choice | Legacy |

### When do you choose managed Flink?

Choose managed Flink for any production workload that is stateful, event-time sensitive, needs complex logic, or is expected to grow.

```java
package com.bank.flink.aws;

import org.apache.flink.table.api.EnvironmentSettings;
import org.apache.flink.table.api.TableEnvironment;

public class ManagedFlinkSqlDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Even SQL-style logic runs on managed Flink
        // with the full engine underneath
        TableEnvironment tEnv = TableEnvironment.create(
            EnvironmentSettings.inStreamingMode());

        tEnv.executeSql(
            "SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) " +
            "FROM transactions " +
            "GROUP BY account_id"
        );
        // Full Flink SQL: temporal joins, MATCH_RECOGNIZE,
        // CDC, watermarks, state TTL all available
    }
}
```

### When is the SQL-only service acceptable?

Choose SQL-only only for very simple, low-stakes transformations where its constraints do not bite and the team wants the absolute minimum setup.

```text
Acceptable SQL-only use cases:
  - Simple filter: route high-value transactions to an alert stream
  - Basic count: count events per minute for a dashboard
  - Quick prototype: test an idea before building a real pipeline

Not acceptable:
  - Fraud detection (needs state, patterns, exactly-once)
  - CDC synchronization (needs changelog semantics)
  - Financial aggregation (needs event-time correctness)
  - Anything production-critical and long-lived
```

### Why does starting on managed Flink avoid rework?

Outgrowing the SQL-only service means a complete rewrite because the programming models are incompatible. Starting on managed Flink, even with Flink SQL, gives you room to grow.

```text
Growth path:
  SQL-only service → need more features → REWRITE to Flink
  Managed Flink (SQL) → need more features → add DataStream code
                                              (same engine, no rewrite)

Managed Flink + Flink SQL gives you:
  - SQL simplicity for simple queries
  - Full engine underneath when you need temporal joins, CEP, etc.
  - No rewrite required as requirements grow
```

### What is the migration path?

AWS encourages migration from SQL-only to managed Flink. The path involves rewriting the SQL into Flink SQL or DataStream code.

```text
Migration steps:
  1. Identify SQL-only queries and their input/output streams
  2. Rewrite as Flink SQL (often 1:1 translation for simple queries)
  3. Add watermarks, state TTL, and proper sink configuration
  4. Deploy on managed Flink
  5. Validate output matches the old SQL-only results
  6. Decommission the SQL-only application
```

### What should a senior engineer know?

- Default new, production-bound work to managed Flink, even when it starts simple.
- Managed Flink supports Flink SQL, so you can still write SQL without the SQL-only service.
- The SQL-only service's simplicity is real but shallow; its weak state and event-time handling make it unsuitable for correctness-sensitive processing.
- Consider cost: managed Flink uses KPU pricing, SQL-only uses a similar model, but managed Flink gives far more capability per unit.
- Keep skills portable by writing standard Flink code that runs on both managed and self-managed clusters.

```java
// Senior tip: use Flink SQL on managed Flink
// Gets the SQL simplicity the team wants
// Plus the full engine: temporal joins, CDC, CEP, exactly-once
// No ceiling, no rewrite risk
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The two AWS offerings differ in power and programming model. Managed Flink runs full Apache Flink applications with the complete feature set: event-time processing, keyed state, CEP, temporal joins, Flink SQL, and exactly-once guarantees. The SQL-only Kinesis Analytics is a legacy service with limited windowing, no real state management, and no event-time handling, suitable only for very simple transforms.

Choose managed Flink for any production workload that is stateful, event-time sensitive, or expected to grow. Managed Flink itself supports Flink SQL, so you get SQL simplicity without the ceiling, making the SQL-only service largely redundant. Outgrowing SQL-only means a complete rewrite, while growing on managed Flink is incremental.

At the National Bank of India, a quick filter routing high-value transactions to an alert stream was acceptable on SQL-only. But the real fraud engine needed per-account state, event-time windows, pattern detection, and exactly-once guarantees, so we built it on managed Flink. We defaulted all new production work to managed Flink, even when it started simple, precisely because growth would otherwise force a rewrite.

Remember one sentence: default to managed Flink for anything production-bound because it gives you the full engine with SQL simplicity, while the SQL-only service is a legacy convenience whose weak state and event-time handling make it unsuitable for correctness-sensitive work.
